tips.title: Five numbers make a box plot
tips.body: **Minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, maximum.** The box runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile, the line inside it is the median, and the whiskers reach out to the two ends. Everything on the diagram is one of those five.

tips.title: The box holds the middle half
tips.body: A quarter of the data sits in each section: below the box, in each half of the box, and above it. So the **box is the middle 50%**, and its **width is the interquartile range**. A narrow box means consistent data.

tips.title: Quartiles are medians of the halves
tips.body: Find the **median** first. The **lower quartile** is the median of the values below it, and the **upper quartile** the median of the values above it. When $n$ is odd, leave the median itself out of both halves.

tips.title: Compare twice, in context
tips.body: A *compare* question wants **two** statements: one about an **average** (the medians) and one about **spread** (the IQRs), each written **in the context** of the question. "B’s median mark is higher, so B did better on average" earns the mark; "B is higher" does not.

tips.title: Prefer the IQR to the range
tips.body: The **range** uses the two most extreme values, so one unusual result changes it completely. The **interquartile range** ignores the top and bottom quarters, so it is not thrown by an outlier. That is why comparisons of spread normally use the IQR.

why.matters:
A box plot throws almost everything away. Out of a hundred numbers it keeps five, and draws them.

That is not a weakness, it is the design. A box plot exists to be put **beside another one**. Two histograms side by side are hard work; two box plots on one scale answer "which is typically higher", "which is more spread out" and "which has something odd at the end" in a single glance, and those three questions are most of what comparing two sets of data ever means.

The five numbers are chosen so that a single freak value cannot move them. That is why the middle line is the median rather than the mean, and why the box is the middle half rather than the whole range.

examples.title: Two routes, and the one you take
examples.body:
The same journey, two ways: the motorway, or the shorter run through town. A month of each, drawn on one scale.

The town route has the lower median — 27 minutes against 28. On a typical day it is quicker, and if the median were all you looked at you would take it every time.

Now look at the boxes. The motorway's interquartile range is 4 minutes; the town's is 14. A quarter of town journeys take more than 36 minutes, which is worse than the motorway's **worst** day of 34. At its worst the town route took 58 minutes — 24 minutes longer than anything the motorway ever did.

So the answer depends on the question. Going to see a friend, take the town route: it is usually quicker. Catching a flight, take the motorway, because you are not buying the typical journey, you are buying the bad one. A box plot is the shape that makes that difference visible, and an average is the shape that hides it.

examples.title: The street with one mansion on it
examples.body:
Eleven houses on one street. Ten of them sold for between £250k and £400k, and one — a converted rectory at the end — went for £3,200k.

The mean price is £583.6k. That figure is higher than 10 of the 11 houses. As a description of the street it is not slightly off, it is useless: no house on it is worth anything like that, and nobody looking to move there would be helped by it.

The median is £325k, which is an actual house on the street. Take the rectory out of the list altogether and the median shifts by £7.5k, to £317.5k. The mean shifts by £261.6k, from £583.6k down to £322k. One of those two statistics noticed the mansion; the other was defined by it.

The range tells the same story: £2,950k, against an interquartile range of £95k — 31 times bigger. This is why house prices, salaries and waiting times are reported as medians and quartiles, and it is why a box plot draws the whiskers separately from the box instead of stretching the box to fit.

steps.title: What a box plot shows
steps.body:
**A box plot draws five numbers from a data set on a scale:**

1. the **minimum**
2. the **lower quartile**, $Q_1$ — a quarter of the way through the data
3. the **median**, $Q_2$ — halfway through
4. the **upper quartile**, $Q_3$ — three quarters of the way through
5. the **maximum**

The **box** runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile. The **line inside** the box is the median. The **whiskers** stretch from the box out to the minimum and the maximum.

**Each section holds a quarter of the data.** Below the box, in the left half of the box, in the right half of the box, above the box: 25% each. That gives two things worth reading off at a glance:

- The **box** contains the **middle 50%** of the data.
- The **width of the box** is the **interquartile range**, $Q_3 - Q_1$ — the spread of that middle half.

**The plot below has** minimum 5, lower quartile 9, median 14, upper quartile 20 and maximum 26. So its range is $26 - 5 = 21$, its IQR is $20 - 9 = 11$, and half of the values lie between 9 and 20.

**A box plot deliberately does not show every value.** It shows the shape of the data — where the middle is, how spread out it is, and whether it is bunched or stretched at either end — which is exactly what is wanted when two sets are to be compared.

steps.title: Finding the five numbers from a list
steps.body:
**Put the data in order first.** Nothing else works until it is sorted.

Then the **median** is the middle value. Each **quartile is the median of the half on its side**. When there is an odd number of values, the median itself is **left out** of both halves. When the number is even, the median is the mean of the two middle values, and each half is simply the half.

steps.title: Comparing two box plots
steps.body:
**Drawn on the same scale, two box plots can be compared by eye, and the exam asks for exactly two comparisons:**

- one about **average**: compare the **medians**
- one about **spread**: compare the **interquartile ranges** (or ranges)

**Each comparison must be in context.** The mark is for saying what the numbers mean about the situation, not for reading them off.

steps.title: Why the IQR, and what the shape tells you
steps.body:
**The range depends on the two most extreme values.** One student who happened to have a terrible day can double it. The **interquartile range** ignores the top and bottom quarters entirely, so a single unusual value cannot change it. That is why the IQR is the measure of spread to prefer when the data may contain an **outlier**, and why exam questions normally expect it.

**The box plot also shows the shape of the data.**

- If the median sits in the **middle of the box** and the whiskers are similar, the data is roughly **symmetrical**.
- If the median is **closer to the lower quartile** and the right whisker is long, the data is **bunched at the low end** with a tail of high values — **positively skewed**.
- The reverse, with a long left whisker, is **negatively skewed**.

**An outlier is a value far from the rest.** Some questions mark outliers as separate points beyond the whiskers; for this course you need to **recognise** an outlier and know that it affects the range and the mean but not the median or IQR, which is one reason those two are the measures of choice.

**Reading percentages off a box plot.** Because each section is a quarter of the data:

- **25%** of values lie above the upper quartile
- **50%** lie inside the box
- **75%** lie below the upper quartile

If a box plot of 40 students has an upper quartile of 20 marks, then $25\%$ of 40 is **10 students** scored more than 20. The box plot never shows the individual values, but it shows exactly how many are in each quarter.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Sort before anything else.** Every wrong quartile in this topic starts with an unsorted list. Write the ordered list down, count it, and mark the middle.

**Odd and even are handled differently, and the difference is examined.** With an **odd** count the median is a single value and is **left out** of both halves before the quartiles are found. With an **even** count the median is the mean of the two middle values, and each half is just the half. Mixing these up moves a quartile by half a place, which is usually enough to lose the mark.

**Two comparisons, each in context.** A *compare* question is looking for one statement about **average** and one about **spread**, and each must say what it means for the situation. *B’s median is higher, so B did better on average* and *B’s IQR is smaller, so B was more consistent* is the complete answer. A third statement about the range adds nothing if the IQR has been used, and a statement that just reads a number off earns nothing.

**Say "more consistent", not "better".** A smaller spread is not automatically better — it depends on the question. A shop wanting predictable delivery times prefers the small IQR; a coach looking for one outstanding runner might not. Interpret the spread in the way the context asks.

**The box plot hides the count.** It shows proportions, not numbers. Two box plots can look identical and describe 12 people and 12 000 people. So a claim like *more students in B scored over 25* cannot be made from the plots alone unless the two class sizes are known — you can say a **larger proportion** did.

**Know what an outlier does.** It stretches the range and drags the mean, and it leaves the median and the IQR alone. That is the whole argument for preferring the median and IQR when the data may contain one, and it is worth stating explicitly when a question asks which measure to use.

**Shape is a reading too.** A median off-centre in its box and one long whisker means the data is **skewed** towards the long side. Being able to say *the data is positively skewed, with most values low and a tail of high ones* is a grade 9 sentence.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A box plot shows **five numbers**: minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, maximum.
- The **box** runs from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$; the **line inside** is the median; the **whiskers** reach the ends.
- **Each section holds a quarter** of the data, so the box is the **middle 50%**.
- The **width of the box is the IQR**: $Q_3 - Q_1$.
- **Sort the data first.** The median is the middle; each quartile is the **median of its half**.
- **Odd count**: leave the median out of both halves. **Even count**: the median is the mean of the two middle values.
- **Compare** with two statements: **medians** for average, **IQRs** for spread, each **in context**.
- *Higher median, so better on average. Smaller IQR, so more consistent.*
- A **reading** is not a comparison; a comparison without **context** earns nothing.
- Prefer the **IQR** to the range, because an **outlier** does not affect it.
- An outlier changes the **range and mean**, not the **median and IQR**.
- The plot shows **proportions**, not counts: 25% above the upper quartile, whatever $n$ is.
- With $n$ known, 25% of $n$ is the number in each quarter.
- **Skew**: median near $Q_1$ with a long right whisker is **positive skew**.
- Smaller spread means **more consistent**, which is not always **better** — interpret the context.

questions.prompt: Explain how to find the five-number summary of a list of data, how each part of a box plot is drawn from it, and why the interquartile range is usually preferred to the range as a measure of spread.
questions.solution:
The five-number summary is the **minimum**, the **lower quartile**, the **median**, the **upper quartile** and the **maximum**.

Everything starts with **sorting the data**. The median and the quartiles are positions in the ordered list, so nothing can be found until it is in order.

The **median** is the middle value. With an **odd** number of values it is the single value in the middle; with an **even** number it is the mean of the two middle values. For 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 30, 34 there are 11 values, so the median is the 6th, which is 22.

Each **quartile is the median of the half on its side**. The lower quartile is the median of the values below the overall median, and the upper quartile is the median of the values above it. When the count is **odd**, the median itself is **left out** of both halves, so each half of the 11 values contains five: 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 gives a lower quartile of 15, and 24, 25, 27, 30, 34 gives an upper quartile of 27. When the count is **even**, the halves are simply the two halves of the list. Getting this odd/even detail wrong shifts a quartile by half a place.

The **box plot** is drawn from those five numbers on a scale. The **box** runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile. A **line inside the box** marks the median. The **whiskers** extend from each end of the box to the minimum and the maximum.

Because each of the four sections holds a **quarter of the data**, the box contains the **middle 50%**, and its width is the **interquartile range**, $Q_3 - Q_1 = 27 - 15 = 12$ here.

The **range** is the maximum minus the minimum, $34 - 12 = 22$. It uses only the two most extreme values, so a **single unusual result** — one student who had a very bad or very good day — can change it completely. The **interquartile range** ignores the lowest quarter and the highest quarter altogether, so an outlier at either end has no effect on it whatsoever. The IQR therefore describes the spread of the **typical** data rather than the spread of its two most unusual points, which is why it is the measure normally preferred, and why it pairs naturally with the median, which is unaffected by outliers for the same reason.

Describes how the box, median line and whiskers are drawn from the five numbers.

questions.prompt: Class A’s test marks have median 22 and interquartile range 12. Class B’s have median 25 and interquartile range 7.5. Both classes sat the same test. Compare the two classes, and explain what a box plot of each class could and could not tell you about how many students scored over 30.
questions.solution:
A comparison of two distributions needs two things: a statement about **average** and a statement about **spread**, each interpreted in the context of the question.

**Average.** Class B’s median is 25 and Class A’s is 22. B’s median is **higher**, so **on average, Class B scored better on the test**. Simply writing that B’s median is 25 would be a reading, not a comparison, and would earn nothing; the mark is for saying what the difference means.

**Spread.** Class B’s interquartile range is 7.5 and Class A’s is 12. B’s IQR is **smaller**, so the middle half of B’s marks are bunched more tightly together: **Class B’s marks were more consistent**. It is important to say *more consistent* rather than *better*. A smaller spread is not a good thing in itself — it means the class performed more uniformly, which may or may not be what a teacher wants. Here it means fewer very low marks in B, but also fewer very high ones relative to their median.

Putting the two together: Class B did better on average and more consistently than Class A.

**What a box plot could tell you about scoring over 30.** A box plot is drawn from the five-number summary, and each section of it holds a **quarter of the data**. So if 30 happened to be one of the plotted values — say Class A’s upper quartile — the plot would say that **25% of Class A** scored above 30. It would also show whether **anyone** in each class scored over 30 at all, from where the maximum whisker ends. Those are statements about **proportions**.

**What it could not tell you** is **how many** students that is. The plot has no scale for the number of values; two classes of 12 and 120 could produce identical plots. To turn 25% into a count you would need to know the **size of the class**, which is not on the diagram. Nor could it tell you how many scored over 30 if 30 fell somewhere inside a section, because within a quarter the individual values are not shown at all.

So from the plots alone the honest claim is that *a larger proportion* of one class scored over 30, never that *more students* did.

A comparison of two distributions needs two things: a statement about **average** and a statement about **spread**, each interpreted in the context of the question.

**Average.** Class B’s median is 25 and Class A’s is 22. B’s median is **higher**, so **on average, Class B scored better on the test**. Simply writing that B’s median is 25 would be a reading, not a comparison, and would earn nothing; the mark is for saying what the difference means.

**Spread.** Class B’s interquartile range is 7.5 and Class A’s is 12. B’s IQR is **smaller**, so the middle half of B’s marks are bunched more tightly together: **Class B’s marks were more consistent**. It is important to say *more consistent* rather than *better*. A smaller spread is not a good thing in itself — it means the class performed more uniformly, which may or may not be what a teacher wants. Here it means fewer very low marks in B, but also fewer very high ones relative to their median.

examTechnique.body:
**Sort the data, find the median, then take the median of each half** — leaving the median out of both halves when the count is odd.

A *compare* question wants **two** sentences: **medians** for average and **IQRs** for spread, each saying what it means **in context**. Reading a number off is not a comparison, and a smaller IQR means **more consistent**, not better.
examinerErrors: Finding the median of the list **as given**, without sorting it.
Including the median in both halves when the count is **odd**.
Reading off two numbers instead of **comparing** them.
Comparing without saying what it means **in context**.
Calling a smaller IQR "better" rather than **more consistent**.
Claiming **how many** people from a plot that shows only **proportions**.
Using the range when an **outlier** makes the IQR the right choice.
Confusing the **box width** (IQR) with the whisker span (range).
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer **sorts first**, handles the **odd/even** difference correctly, and gives quartiles as decimals when that is what the halves produce. On a *compare* question it writes exactly **two interpreted sentences** — average from the medians, spread from the IQRs — and says *more consistent* rather than *better*. It knows the plot shows **proportions, not counts**, so it claims a *larger proportion* rather than *more people* unless the group size is given. It prefers the **IQR** when an outlier is possible and can say why, and it reads **skew** from where the median sits in its box.
